In the torus case, it is known that the attractor is a band as shown in
ﬁg (3) ([Martins, 2004]); and on a 2-hole torus, from the discussion above,
there can be at most 3 attractors.
Assume it is true for the genus-p surface such that it has (2p−1) invariant

Inversely Unstable Solutions of
Two-Dimensional Systems on Genus-p
Surfaces and the Topology of Knotted
Attractors

So generally speaking, a dissipative system given by (17) that situated
on a genus-p surface can have at most p topologically distinct knotted at-
tractors; whether they are homeomorphic to a circle individually depends
on the existence of inversely unstable solution within themselves.
It is known that any dynamical system sitting on a 2-manifold with
p genus can be represented on a sphere by cutting each handle along a
fundamental circuit which contains no equilibrium point and ﬁlling in the
dynamics within the resulting region bounded by these curves (see [Banks,
2002]).
Conversely, we can get higher genus surface systems by performing surgery
on certain spherical ones. Speciﬁcally, given a spherical system, irrespective
of the rest of the dynamics, as long as it contains 2 stable equilibria, we can
choose a small neighbourhood Mi (i = 1, 2) around each of them such that
they are the only equilibrium points within each region. Glue in a dissipa-
tive region with attractor A as in ﬁg (14), cut this attractor open, twist it
and identify the two ends together in the appropriate way, we then obtain
the desired knot. If the attractor contains an inversely unstable solution,
then it is not homeomorphic to a circle, which means chaotic behaviour will
occur within this invariant set.
Hence we have proved

We have studied dynamical systems on a genus-p surface and extend the
generalized automorphic functions (see [Banks & Song, 2006]) to deﬁne a
general form for these systems (both analytic and non-analytic). Also we
look at the topology of knotted attractors under the existence of unstable
periodic orbits and prove that for a genus-p surface with only one unstable
cycle, the number of invariant sets may vary while a maximum of (2p −1)
must not be exceeded. Moreover, we extend the result in [Martins, 2004] and
show that for a higher genus (genus > 1) surface, the individual attractor
is not homeomorphic to a circle if there exists an inversely unstable solution
within itself. This is purely because of the property of inversely unstable
solution which can generate a local behaviour to make the dynamics ﬁght
against the eﬀect of global unstable orbit.
In the future paper, we will consider automorphic functions in 3-dimension
which will give us systems naturally deﬁned on genus-p solid 3-manifolds.

The corpus search resolved cleanly. One document is overwhelmingly the answer, with two others touching "genus" in unrelated senses. Here's the complete answer.

## Answer: "genus surfaces topology"

The corpus contains one paper squarely about the **topology of genus surfaces**, plus two that use "genus" in unrelated technical senses.

### Primary source — `0706.2397.pdf`
**"Inversely Unstable Solutions of Two-Dimensional Systems on Genus-p Surfaces and the Topology of Knotted Attractors"** (p. 1). This paper studies dynamical systems living on higher-genus surfaces and the topology of their attractors:

- **Core setup (p. 2):** A periodic 2-D time-varying oscillator with damping has an invariant set that is *not homeomorphic to a circle* when an inversely unstable solution exists. The paper generalizes this so that several attractors can coexist and be "linked in a higher genus surface on which the system is defined," and studies the topology of those attractors. It also cites Banks (2002) for expressing a system on a **genus-p surface** in terms of a spherical one by "opening each handle" — cutting along a fundamental circuit with no equilibria and adding fixed points on the resulting sphere (p. 2).

- **Genus-2 case (p. 10):** For genus-2 surfaces, cutting a 2-hole torus along a knotted trajectory topologically turns the surface into a torus with 2 boundary circles.

- **Counting attractors (p. 11):** By induction — the torus attractor is a band, a 2-hole torus admits at most 3 attractors, and adding one unit of genus introduces another hole giving at most two more attractors — a **genus-p surface has at most (2p−1) invariant sets**.

- **Main theorem (p. 14):** A dissipative system on a genus-p surface has at most *p* topologically distinct knotted attractors; whether each is homeomorphic to a circle depends on the existence of an inversely unstable solution within it. Any dynamical system on a p-genus 2-manifold can be represented on a sphere by cutting each handle; conversely, higher-genus systems are built by surgery on spherical ones (gluing in a dissipative region, cutting the attractor, twisting, and re-identifying the ends to form a knot).

- **Conclusion (p. 19):** Systems on a genus-p surface, with only one unstable cycle, have a number of invariant sets that may vary but must not exceed (2p−1); for genus > 1, an individual attractor is not homeomorphic to a circle if it contains an inversely unstable solution. Future work targets automorphic functions in 3-D giving systems on genus-p solid 3-manifolds.

### Secondary / tangential mentions
- **`0706.0028.pdf` (pp. 12, 32):** Uses "genus" in Morse-theory context — a surface "of genus g ≥ 2" with its Reeb graph ΓF (p. 12) — and mentions the C²-topology on C∞(M) (p. 32). "Genus" and "topology" appear but not as the paper's subject; it's about Reeb graphs of functions on surfaces.
- **`0709.2857.pdf` (p. 3):** "Genus" here is the **Todd genus** (algebraic geometry / characteristic classes), invoked via the topological Euler characteristic and Leray–Hirsch theorem — unrelated to surface genus.

### Bottom line
If you want genus, surfaces, and topology together as a single subject, the answer is entirely in **`0706.2397.pdf`**: dynamical systems on genus-p surfaces, with the key results that such a surface supports at most **p** knotted attractors / **(2p−1)** invariant sets, and that an attractor fails to be homeomorphic to a circle precisely when an inversely unstable solution is present (pp. 1, 2, 10, 11, 14, 19).

*(Note: search ran in keyword mode — semantic embeddings weren't available in this environment — but coverage was full: all 100/100 docs were searched.)*
